events.title: We built a life we love states away from our parents. Now that we're starting a family, I'm second-guessing our choice.
events.summary: We moved away from our parents and built our dream life in Colorado. Now that we're beginning to grow our family, I'm questioning our decision. Lexi Marshall My husband and I love the life we built in Colorado, but we're far from my parents and his. We've managed the distance with trips and calls, but I'm worried about it as we grow our family. I don't want to move, but I worry about having our future kids grow up without grandparents nearby . For years, moving to Colorado felt like the easiest decision in the world. My husband and I both came here on our own, drawn by the mountains, the outdoor lifestyle, and the possibility of building a life somewhere that felt more like us. I moved to Colorado 10 years ago; he followed five years ago. We met here, fell in love here, and eventually built the kind of life we'd once imagined from afar. Now we're starting a family, and for the first time, I'm wondering if we've built our dream life too far away from the people who raised us. Our families are rooted somewhere else We love spending time in Colorado with our dogs, but I wish we had family nearby. Lexi Marshall My parents live in the Chicago suburbs, where both sides of my family have lived for generations. There are decades of history there: grandparents, aunts and uncles, family traditions , familiar streets. My husband's family is in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and his siblings are there, too, along with their children. That means our future children won't just have grandparents who live far away; they'll have cousins who live far away, too. A Pew Research Center survey found that 75% of American adults consider it at least somewhat important to live in a community where family is nearby. I used to understand that statistic in the abstract. Now, as we're preparing to have a child, I understand it differently. I've always understood that choosing Colorado meant giving up some proximity to family. But when it was just the two of us, that trade-off felt more manageable. We could fly home for the holiday s. We could plan trips around birthdays. We could FaceTime when we missed someone. We had the freedom to pack a bag and go. Having children makes the distance feel different. As much as I love our life in this area of the US, I wonder if living here for the long run is the right call. Lexi Marshall Suddenly, I'm picturing the ordinary moments, not just the big ones: grandparents stopping by for dinner, cousins playing together on a random Saturday, my parents being close enough to help when we're overwhelmed. I'm thinking about all the memories that happen without anyone planning them. One 2026 Marquette Law School poll of about 1,500 adults in the US found that 56% of grandparents with adult children living within 50 miles cared for a grandchild at least once a month. Among grandparents whose adult children all lived more than 50 miles away, that figure fell to 18%. Suddenly, the difference between "we can visit" and "we can swing by" feels pretty significant. The life we chose is still the life we love We've come to love Colorado, even on the days we're most aware of the miles between family and us. Lexi Marshall The complicated part is that I don't actually want to leave Colorado. This is home. It's where my husband and I met. It's where we've spent years building our relationship, careers, friendships, routines, and community. The mountains that initially brought us here aren't just scenery anymore — they're part of our everyday life. And there's something uncomfortable about questioning a decision that, for so long, felt so unquestionably right. Part of me worries that I'm romanticizing what it would be like to live closer to family . Being nearby doesn't automatically mean everyone will have the time, energy, or ability to show up. Families have their own lives, schedules, challenges, and routines. And moving closer wouldn't recreate the exact childhood or extended-family experience I remember growing up, since my husband's and my parents don't even live in the same state. Maybe there's no perfect version of this decision I'm not eager to leave a place I love so much. Lexi Marshall I suspect this is one of those choices that becomes more complicated once you're a parent: You can be grateful for the life you've created and still wonder about the life you didn't choose. I don't know yet what the answer is. Maybe we'll stay in Colorado and find ways to make the distance work. Maybe we'll eventually move closer to one of our families. Maybe we'll spend years going back and forth before we figure out what feels right. What I do know is that starting a family has changed the way I think about "home." For a decade, home meant Colorado to me. It meant mountains and independence and the life my husband and I intentionally created together. Now I'm realizing that home might also be measured in grandparents' houses, cousins' birthdays, family dinners , and the people who can show up when you need them. I don't regret moving to Colorado — not even a little. But for the first time, I'm allowing myself to admit that the dream life we chose comes with a trade-off … and I'm not sure yet how much that trade-off will matter once our family gets bigger. events.title: Netherlands moves billions in gold to London in 'crisis preparedness' move
events.summary: While much of the gold was sold in New York and then repurchased in London, more than 27 tonnes was physically moved to the UK The Dutch central bank (DNB) has confirmed that billions of dollars in gold has been taken out of north America and relocated to London, citing "increasing geopolitical unrest". DNB said on Wednesday that 86 tonnes of gold had been removed from the US and Canada in a complex operation that took several months. It is now being held by the Bank of England, where the precious metal can be traded more easily "in a crisis situation". Bank president Olaf Sleijpen said the move was "necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness". The decision comes amid an ongoing trade dispute between the US and Canada, with both countries announcing fresh tariffs on each other after failed trade talks. DNB said the transfer, which took place between March and August, saw 27 tonnes of gold bars moved from New York and Ottawa to Zeist in the Netherlands. A similar quantity and quality was then moved to London, with no need to melt the bars down. Exactly how so much gold was transported across the Atlantic Ocean has not been revealed. The rest of the transfer was carried out by selling the gold in New York, and repurchasing it in London, the bank said , external . "Combining the processes of buying and selling and physical transport has allowed DNB to spread the risks associated with such a complex physical gold relocation," the statement said. DNB did not confirm what it was referring to with its mention of "geopolitical unrest" but the US economy remains in an uncertain position due to the country's ongoing war with Iran, which has impacted global trade. Canada, meanwhile, has been hit hard by US tariffs on its key sectors of steel, aluminium, lumber and automobiles as well as an additional 50% levy on about C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) of Canadian goods announced in August. DNB said that gold that is held with the Bank of England "is regarded as the world's most easily tradable gold," and therefore more readily available in a crisis than if it was still in the US or Canada. Prior to Wednesday's announcement, the DNB held 31.3% of its gold in New York and 19.7% in Ottawa. This has now fallen to 18.5% in both countries. The total Dutch gold stock was 612.4 tonnes at the end of 2025 and has been valued at €72.2 billion, DNB said. The bank's share of gold in London has increased from 18.1% to 32.1% after the move, while it still holds 30.8% of its reserves in the Netherlands. events.title: Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget | Nils Pratley
events.summary: Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget Fair to say the current sell-off is international, but the PM has said little yet to make investors rethink the UK’s status I t’s too soon to say the bond markets have turned on Andy Burnham. Tuesday’s spike in gilt yields, taking the UK’s 30-year borrowing costs to their highest level since 1998 , was part of an international sell-off of government debt . The main contributors are well known. The Iran war, by increasing the cost of energy, has overturned the comforting start-of-the-year thesis of falling global inflation and interest rates. A plunging Japanese yen has kicked away another assumed source of financial stability. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, hasn’t calmed nerves with his solo, and so far futile, attempt to bring down US yields . Meanwhile, the early stage of the AI revolution is an exercise in issuing squillions of debt before long-term returns on capital can possibly be assessed meaningfully. From the point of view of the mythical bond vigilante , in these circumstances it’s only logical to demand a higher return to lend to profligate governments with high debt ratios, which is most of them. In a narrow sense, then, UK gilts were just moving with the market at a moment of rising financial risks in all directions. It’s just that the UK was already uncomfortably placed at the cold edge of the pack with the highest borrowing rates in the G7, a status largely reflecting a dismal 20-year record in keeping a lid on inflation and, especially now, a dependency on energy imports that stood at 43% in 2025. It is also true, unfortunately, that six weeks into the job Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, have said nothing to make bond investors rethink the UK’s status. Investors have heard the dutiful commitment to Rachel Reeves’s fiscal rules, but Burnham’s Commons speech on Tuesday carried little sense of urgency about the UK’s financial predicament, or appreciation of how 10-year gilt yields at 5.2% will cause damage if sustained for long. More “public control” of utilities – the theme Burnham constantly returns to – may be desirable and play well on the backbenches. But, even when the ambiguous meaning is made clearer, how does it translate into, say, substantially lower costs of building infrastructure? Should it really be a top economic priority? “Markets are sceptical that ‘devolution’ and ‘control’ are levers for lower government-led inflation,” said the Panmure Liberum economist Simon French. “Burnham/Healey’s unenviable task is to prove they are the right levers. If they fail then a very painful period of financial repression/demand side-led disinflation will be necessary.” There is an uncomfortable sense that the bond market expects next month’s budget to be a bigger event than Burnham and Healey will produce. The tone of Burnham’s Commons speech was “the last thing investors wanted to hear”, said the former Goldman Sachs economist Jim O’Neill – quite a verdict from a friendly critic who was being lined up for a role in government until recently. But one can see his point. He told the BBC that high government borrowing costs would force Labour to get real about dealing with the triple lock on the state pension and “excessive” welfare spending. There has been little rolling of the pitch, as they say in Westminster, in either of those directions to date. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning It may be, of course, that impressions are mistaken and that next month’s promised 10-year economic plan turns out to be a big exercise in addressing energy costs, defence spending, social care, housing shortages and all the other main challenges. But it is also easy to imagine an alternative script in which hard decisions are deferred and the UK-specific action in the bond market turns uglier – especially if, say, disruption to global energy markets looks likely to last the winter. Labour has spent 2026 defenestrating one leader and anointing another. It needs something to show for it. Burnham speaks of giving businesses and consumers breathing space from the cost of living pressures. That task is easier when the government itself is getting some breathing space from the bond markets. Whatever the chosen mix of spending cuts and tax rises, the budget needs details.

events.title: X shifts US creator payouts from Stripe to X Money
events.summary: Elon Musk’s social network X on Wednesday said that starting today, all of its U.S. creator payouts will be handled through X Money, the app’s payments service. This includes payouts from both X’s Original Content Rewards Program and creators’ subscriptions, the company said in an update shared on X. Starting today, U.S. payouts for Original Content Rewards and Subscriptions will be paid through @XMoney . You'll have access to your payouts the moment they’re sent. › Already using 𝕏 Money? No action needed. Your next payout will be sent there. › Not yet on 𝕏 Money? Open… — Creators (@XCreators) September 2, 2026 The benefit of this new payment system is that the payments are instant. There’s no waiting until the end of a billing cycle or a minimum threshold that has to be reached before the creator can access their money. Previously, payments were processed every two weeks, with a minimum payout of $30, X’s documentation states . However, the announcement’s wording seems to indicate that there aren’t any other options for receiving payments on the platform, meaning X is forcing creators to use X Money even if they would have preferred the prior payout method, which was powered by Stripe . Reached for comment, a representative for X said the change is required for those in the U.S. Creators outside the U.S. will remain on Stripe. The shift follows other changes to X’s creator programs. On September 7, X will retire its Creator Revenue Sharing Program, which stopped accepting new members last month. Creators are being shifted instead to the Original Content Rewards Program, which, as the name implies, puts a heavier emphasis on original content . The company’s new payments service, X Money , began supporting creator payouts earlier this month. The payments offering, a part of Musk’s broader plan to make X an “ everything app ,” includes a bank card with 3% cash back, instant payments, free ATM withdrawals, and other digital banking services. However, X Money is not a bank; the accounts are held at the FDIC-insured Cross River Bank. X’s post said creator payouts will also count toward X Money users’ direct deposit requirements to receive the service’s better APY rate. Currently, the service’s website says X Premium users will get a boosted 6% rate, compared to the standard 4% rate. In addition, X will issue a 1099-NEC for individuals receiving creator payouts. For LLCs, X will collect the organization’s W-9 information to ensure the 1099s are accurate, the company noted . This article was updated after publication with X’s comment. events.title: US government sides with OpenAI on issue of training LLMs on copyrighted material
events.summary: In a lawsuit that The New York Times filed against OpenAI, the Trump administration has contributed a 20-page brief in defense of the ChatGPT maker’s unlicensed use of copyrighted material to train its LLMs. “The United States has a strong interest in continuing to develop a robust and competitive artificial intelligence industry that sets the standard for the practice and procedure of AI use globally… As such, it is critical for the United States to ‘retain global leadership in artificial intelligence,’” the brief reads, referencing an executive order that President Donald Trump signed last year. The LLMs powering chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are trained on incomprehensibly massive databases of published works, including copyrighted books, articles, and other media that AI companies feed into these databases without permission. Many publishers, including The New York Times in this case, have sought to argue that it is illegal for AI companies like OpenAI to train AI models on their copyrighted material. This question — can you use copyrighted material to train an AI? — isn’t black and white, hence the extensive legal debate around the subject. These conversations often center on fair use, a carve out of copyright law that makes exceptions for certain scenarios when it can be ruled legal to use someone else’s copyrighted work without permission. In this case, the fair use debate addresses whether AI companies’ use of copyrighted work is “transformative” enough for a judge to rule it legal. “Constraining LLM development under a misunderstanding of fair use doctrine would thwart such creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility,” the brief says. So far, cases about AI training and copyright infringement have largely been favorable to AI companies. Last year, Judge William Alsup ordered Anthropic to pay a $1.5 billion copyright settlement to a group of writers whose works were used to train the company’s AI models; but Anthropic wasn’t dinged for its AI training. Rather, the company was fined for using illegal shadow libraries to pirate the books it used for training. “Like any reader aspiring to be a writer, Anthropic’s LLMs trained upon works not to race ahead and replicate or supplant them — but to turn a hard corner and create something different,” Judge Alsup wrote, comparing the LLM’s training to a human reading a book. This new Trump administration brief is not a ruling, as the case is being tried in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, and the authors of the brief do not have jurisdiction. However, this intervention by the Trump administration could still carry weight. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Rupert Murdoch 'very happy' to be played by Guy Pearce in new film
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Ink, starring Guy Pearce, is the headline film at this year's Venice Film Festival. ( Reuters: Corey Rudy ) Rupert Murdoch is reportedly "very happy" that Guy Pearce is playing him in a new film, the Australian actor tells the Venice Film Festival. Ink, which charts the Australian-born media mogul's foray into British media, is the headline feature at the festival this year. Director Danny Boyle says the film offers a more sympathetic view of Murdoch's attitudes towards British society. Australian-born media mogul Rupert Murdoch is "very happy" to see compatriot Guy Pearce play him in a new, largely sympathetic movie about his early business life, the actor has told the Venice Film Festival. Pearce, known for his role as a dashing detective in LA Confidential and lately in The Brutalist, was cast by Oscar-winning British director Danny Boyle to play Murdoch in his upcoming film, "Ink". Rift laid bare in Murdoch court documents Newly unsealed court documents reveal how the world's biggest family succession drama played out in court. "I had some messaging with Elisabeth, [Murdoch's] daughter, and she did say to me, 'Dad's very happy that you're playing him,'" Pearce told reporters at the Venice Film Festival, where Ink is the opening film. "But he hadn't seen the film at that point, so we'll see," Pearce added. Hit HBO series Succession was inspired by the Murdoch family, with the ruthless and cruel patriarch Logan Roy providing a hugely unflattering portrait of the real-life billionaire. Boyle, despite his own left-wing politics, said he had not set out to make a negative film about Murdoch, now aged 95. The tycoon's right-wing media empire is still a major political force in Britain, the United States and his native Australia, backing a string of conservative nationalist politicians and their agendas. In Ink, Boyle focuses on Murdoch's move into Britain in the late 1960s, when he bought the struggling tabloid The Sun and transformed it into a runaway success with a daily diet of sex, sport and scandal. Rupert Murdoch's media outlets have long wielded significant political influence in the US, UK and Australia. ( Reuters: Carlo Allegri ) It is an adaptation of a play by British playwright James Graham, which ran in the West End and Broadway between 2017 and 2019. "The stage play doesn't … monsterise Rupert Murdoch, which, of course, a lot of people do now," Boyle said. "I think it's because he represented at the time … a breath of fresh air in what was a very rigid British society. And he's dealing with a lot of prejudice against him as an Australian, which I can understand," the Trainspotting and Slumdog Millionaire director added. Ink follows the relationship between Murdoch and his first editor of The Sun, Larry Lamb, with the latter the main character in the film, Boyle told reporters. Murdoch, his business empire and his feuds with his six children have become rich pickings for authors, screenwriters and directors. As well as Succession, the five-times married tycoon has been the subject of a spate of biographies, as well as a new Netflix documentary, Dynasty: The Murdochs which was released in March this year. The latter focused on Murdoch's fight with his children over efforts to install his eldest son Lachlan as his chosen successor to run an empire comprising Fox News, The Wall Street Journal, The Sun and publisher HarperCollins. The Murdoch family's internal dynamics have been the inspiration of multiple movies and TV shows. ( Reuters: Peter Nicholls ) That ended with a multi-billion-dollar settlement and court case that spilled some of the family's secrets into the public domain. Murdoch has transformed tabloid newspapers, cable TV and satellite broadcasting over the last few decades while facing accusations of stoking nationalist populism across the English-speaking world. Britain's exit from the European Union and the rise of Donald Trump are credited at least partly to Murdoch, while his media have long carried a pro-business agenda and have been sceptical about climate change.

events.title: The US Navy's top admiral says lasers are key to keeping cheap drones from eating into warship missile magazines
events.summary: As the US Navy assesses what weapons it could need in a layered defense against a range of threats, laser weapons could be a promising choice. US Marine Corps photo by Staff Sgt. Donald Holbert The US Navy's top admiral wrote an op-ed saying laser weapons are necessary to counter cheap drones. Lasers and other directed-energy weapons are preferable against low-cost targets. The Navy recognizes that using high-end munitions against cheaper threats is unsustainable. The US Navy's top admiral sees laser weapons as a strategic answer to the cost challenge of combating cheap drones. The Navy has been looking to laser and directed-energy weapons as a potentially cheaper means of neutralizing uncrewed systems, preserving limited and much more expensive interceptor missiles for higher-end threats. Laser weaponry, however, has been tricky to develop, as its effectiveness in combat depends heavily on power, cooling, and other shipboard systems. In a Wednesday op-ed for The Washington Post, Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, identified the cost imbalance of using multimillion-dollar interceptors to take out low-cost drones as a "defining challenge for the US Navy." "Recent conflicts have demonstrated how quickly low-cost drones, one-way attack aircraft and other relatively inexpensive weapons can pressure even advanced air and missile defenses," the admiral explained, cautioning that "a defender who fires multimillion-dollar interceptors against inexpensive drones may win the immediate engagement while losing the larger campaign of endurance." "This is why directed energy weapons — especially high-powered lasers — matter strategically," Caudle said. As the sea service battled the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen from October 2023 to May 2025, Navy warships routinely relied on missiles to eliminate drone threats. The Navy also regularly used top interceptors to combat ballistic missiles, straining stocks. Last year, Adm. James Kilby, the acting chief of naval operations at that time, told Business Insider that the way the service had been heavily leaning on its interceptors in the Middle East would not be sustainable in a high-tempo fight. During his July 2025 confirmation hearing for the CNO position, Caudle told the Senate Committee on Armed Services that the Navy faced a "learning curve" choosing the right weapons . He said that lessons from the Red Sea led the Navy to look to cheaper air-to-air weapons and electronic warfare when possible, but further consideration is necessary. The war with Iran this year, which has seen the US military face both drone and missile threats, has also demonstrated how quickly American forces can expend key stockpiles of high-value defensive munitions . The fighting added to concerns already sharpened by the Red Sea campaign over how long US interceptor stockpiles might last in a lengthy conflict. US personnel used the Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser to shoot down three cartel drones last week. US Army Photo by Sgt. Daniel Huerta While the defense industry is expediting and expanding the production of critical munitions, recent conflicts have turned up the pressure on the military to find more cost-effective, more sustainable solutions for defending against large numbers of drones. Laser weapons are a promising capability to meet that threat and preserve those stockpiles, Caudle wrote, arguing that "lasers offer the possibility of shifting part of naval defense away from finite stored munitions toward shipboard electrical power." That said, "lasers are not magic weapons," he wrote. Lasers are line-of-sight weapons bound by combat realities like the atmosphere, ocean environment, beam strength and accuracy, and power and cooling requirements. To properly support laser weaponry, warships need enough power and the correct coolants to keep it from overheating. That means ship design has to be considered alongside weapon design. Caudle stressed that laser weapons are not a replacement for high-end interceptor missiles. Instead, he added, directed-energy capabilities should be deployed as part of a larger, layered defense, employed against certain lower-cost threats. The admiral said that the Navy needs to start incrementally readying the sea service for laser weaponry with more manageable, self-contained systems on ships rather than waiting for "perfect megawatt-class systems." He said that such systems would not represent a "final answer," but rather "a practical bridge between promising technology and an operational capability the fleet can learn from, improve, and scale." The Navy has been working on laser weapons for years, evaluating them for maritime missions at its Directed Energy Systems Integration Laboratory in California. The sea service installed an early operational laser demonstrator, the Laser Weapon System, on the Austin-class amphibious transport dock USS Ponce in the 2010s, and then it installed a 150kW Solid State Laser Technology Maturation demonstrator, or SSL-TM, on the San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock USS Portland in 2019, using it to successfully destroy a drone target in May 2020 before it was uninstalled in 2023. Additionally, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Preble is equipped with Lockheed Martin's High Energy Laser with Integrated Optical-dazzler and Surveillance, or HELIOS. Lockheed Martin said earlier this year that HELIOS eliminated four drones during a Navy-operated demonstration last year. Some other destroyers are equipped with the lower-powered Optical Dazzling Interdictor , Navy, or ODIN, which is used mainly to disrupt the optical sensors on drones and other threats. Other services have explored the use of lasers as well. Last week, the US Army saw a laser weapons win, using the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser to eliminate three drug cartel-linked drones at the southern US border. EasyJet has rejoined the FTSE 100, but its return could be short-lived after the company agreed to be bought by a private equity firm in a £5.7 billion deal. North Sea oil and gas producer Ithaca Energy has also been promoted, while housebuilder Persimmon and gambling group Entain have dropped out of the UK’s top stock index. The latest quarterly reshuffle was confirmed after the stock markets closed on Wednesday. The budget airline had seen its share price decline after reporting widening losses on its balance sheet. But it has been given a boost in recent months after becoming the subject of a bidding battle between investment firms Apollo and Castlelake. events.title: Democrats make the midterms about one big pitch: Lower costs
events.summary: David’s view House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries shared good news with his caucus this week: His Democrats’ bid for a midterm campaign focused on “affordability” is cutting through the noise. According to polling that Jeffries circulated this week, Democrats have fixed a mismatch that looked glaring five months ago. In April, voters had said that the “cost of living,” “the economy,” and “inflation” were their number one, two, and three issues, respectively — but that ’ top issue was healthcare, with cost of living at No. 3 and the other topics barely registering. Voters now thought that Democrats, like them, were most worried about the cost of living, then healthcare, then the economy. Jeffries then took to the cameras to explain how this agenda would play out next year, if he becomes speaker. “We have to reverse the Medicaid cuts,” the New Yorker told reporters. “We should extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits. We should restore congressional authority, as it relates to tariffs, because the Trump tariffs are making life more expensive for the American people. And we should end, decisively, if it’s still going on, Donald Trump’s reckless and costly war in Iran.” Online pundits promptly panned that plan as too narrow, reflecting a persistent nostalgia for the 1994 “Contract With America” and “Six for ’06″ Democratic platform shaped by Rahm Emanuel and Chuck Schumer. On social media, where nothing Jeffries does is credible, there’s a hunger for Democrats to identify a few specific, popular bills that every candidate can run on this fall. And it won’t be satisfied. Democrats aren’t crafting the kind of bold-faced messaging that excites take-writers this year. Instead they’re promising voters who are paying more for groceries, fuel, vacations, and more that they can get relief by switching from red to blue. This theory isn’t landing in Washington, where the frantic and ideologically charged discourse portrays the adrift Democrats as led around by their left wing. Turn on the TV in a swing seat, though, and you can see its power. The focus in competitive races is, still, on affordability. In New Jersey’s 7th District, which backed Trump by 1 point in 2024, GOP Rep. Tom Kean is running ads about how he “protected Medicare and Medicaid.” In Virginia’s 2nd District, where Trump and Kamala Harris basically tied, GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans sums up the last two years of her party’s trifecta as “lowering prescription drug costs” and cutting taxes. The schedule for next week’s Republican midterm convention — which Democrats think was a terrible idea that they might have accidentally trolled Trump into — shows that President Donald Trump’s party is trying to deliver its own take on an “affordability” message. Republicans will tout their “working families tax cuts,” lower prescription drug prices, and crackdowns on fraud and immigration that haven’t yet made a dent in the national debt. What they’ll also do next week in Dallas, of course, is fill in the blanks of Democrats’ still-broad agenda for a possible House majority. There’s a consensus that a Democratic H.R. 1 next year would focus on some mix of ideas to lower the cost of living — a clear change from the party’s last majority, which started with voting rights as part of its H.R. 1. The five “affordability working groups” appointed by Jeffries, which teamed up more progressive and more moderate Democrats, will hash out the details. Yet in the meantime, Republicans insist that their opponents’ true agenda is being written by Democratic Socialists of America. In reality, there’s no chance that Jeffries would call votes on defunding law enforcement, transgender medical care, or other issues that the GOP warns about. And most Democrats I talked to this week think that his strategy makes sense. After all, what was the GOP’s agenda in 2010 and 2014, the most consequential midterm elections of the conservative revival? Few people can tell you what was in the 2010 Pledge to America. But if you read it now , you get a clear sense of the post-Bush, pre-Trump GOP’s identity, which centered on canceling the first two years of the Obama White House’s healthcare and financial policies – giving voters a pure deregulatory prescription for economic growth. There was a concord between GOP leadership and grassroots activists that’s not really possible for the Democrats of 2026. So that’s why, in lieu of a point-by-point plan, Democrats just want to win the “affordability” argument and convince voters that Trump needs guardrails. Politically motivated redistricting is working against them, but their plan seems to be succeeding. Room for Disagreement Left-wing Democrats are still fretting that party leaders won’t give voters concrete, populist policies. They point out that the most popular applause line by Democrats angling for the next presidential nomination is that their party can’t simply reconstitute the pre-Trump era. But the Jeffries-backed affordability agenda is essentially a promise to wind the clock back to January 2025: fewer tariffs, no war, more healthcare tax credits. Notable NBC News reporter Sahil Kapur, who asked Jeffries that big agenda question on Tuesday, writes more about the agenda, and left-wing frustration that it’s not bolder. In Axios, Andrew Solender covers the two-vote rebellion against Jeffries on the floor this week, and the fury at the rest of the caucus at Blue Dogs who gave Republicans a win. events.title: Enhanced geothermal notches another win as Google buys 400 MW from Fervo
events.summary: Geothermal energy company Fervo notched another win as Google agreed to buy nearly half a gigawatt of electricity to power a planned new data center in Utah. The power purchase agreement, announced Tuesday, commits Google to buying 396 megawatts from Fervo’s Cape Station power plant in Utah, which is expected to come online in 2028. Google has the option through June 2030 to buy an additional 600 megawatts. The deal arrives as Google and other hyperscalers are scouring the country for new sources of electricity. For years, Google has been one of the larger purchasers of c l ean energy in the U.S. and elsewhere, buying electricity from wind, solar, and batteries to make good on its promise to reach net-zero emissions by 2030. But in April, that goal became harder to reach after Google inked a deal with data center developer Crusoe for 933 megawatts of natural gas power in Texas. The Fervo deal could help Google fuel its AI ambitions without significantly imperiling its net-zero goal. Fervo is permitted to develop up to 2 gigawatts of geothermal energy at Cape Station, but Sarah Jewett, Fervo’s senior vice president of strategy, told TechCrunch in May that a third-party engineer said the site holds enough heat to generate twice as much electricity. If fully developed, those 4 gigawatts would about double the entire geothermal generating capacity in the U.S., according to a recent U.S. Department of Energy report . It’s possible that Google’s gigawatt deal could grow even larger if Fervo’s operations go as planned. Enhanced geothermal technologies, like the kind Fervo has developed, can tap deeper sources of heat. Using those technologies, the U.S. could generate up to 57 terawatts of electricity, according to the report. Fervo and Google’s new deal adds to the pair’s long-standing relationship. The companies have been working together for more than five years , with Google buying some of Fervo’s first electrons . Recently, Google invested in Fervo’s last funding round before the geothermal startup went public . Though Fervo’s stock popped on its first day of trading, it shed those gains and more over the last few months. News of the Google deal, though, drove the stock up about 30% yesterday before traders took some profits today. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. He received his PhD in environmental science, policy, and management from the University of California, Berkeley, and his BA degree in environmental studies, English, and biology from St. Olaf College. events.title: Uber to cut over 3,000 jobs in major global restructuring
events.summary: Uber is cutting about 10% of its global workforce, bringing staffing back to levels last seen in 2021. Uber is cutting more than 3,000 jobs worldwide as part of a major overhaul designed to shrink management layers and refocus spending on its core business. The cuts amount to roughly 10% of its global workforce, bringing staffing back to levels last seen in 2021. Chief executive Dara Khosrowshahi told staff in a company email that the taxi and delivery firm had expanded quickly but accumulated too many layers and small teams that slowed decision‑making. He said the reductions would put Uber, which has its global head office in San Francisco, US, in a better position for its "biggest opportunities ahead of us". The move marks one of Uber's largest restructurings in years and signals a shift towards a leaner operating model. Cuts affect both managers and non-managers, and Uber said it plans to fold many of its smallest teams into larger groups, however, the firm has not confirmed the locations most affected by job cuts. Such changes are intended to make Uber "simpler" and "faster," while freeing up money to reinvest in areas it considers central to its future , Khosrowshahi said. The restructuring comes as Uber steps up investment in autonomous vehicle partnerships and expands its ride‑hailing, delivery, and robotaxi operations . Uber is also tightening up its office strategy, asking nearly all employees to work in person at designated hubs and limiting remote roles to about 1%. Analysts said the layoffs could generate up to $2bn in annual savings. Unlike many large technology companies that have cut jobs amid heavy spending on artificial intelligence (AI), Uber had avoided major reductions since the pandemic. The latest changes bring its workforce back to just under 30,000 people, roughly where it stood before its most recent period of expansion. events.title: The $1 Trump coin: legal tender, depending on what you mean by legal
events.summary: Various laws and 250 years of tradition prevent the likeness of living people from appearing on currency. Donald Trump and Scott Bessent don’t want you to worry about that This was originally published in This Week in Trumpland. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday Two hallmarks of Donald Trump ’s second-term: the president’s enthusiasm for putting his name and face on things, and his cavalier approach to established law. Today the president is once again combining both those interests, as the government releases a $1 coin bearing his image , an item of currency that scholars say should be illegal, but which is happening anyway. How many times have you heard that in the last 18 months? The US has had a long tradition of not putting living people on US currencybeginning in the late 1700s when the US Mint, which manufactures and distributes currency, wanted to put an image of George Washington on US money. Washington declined, saying it would be too much like a monarchy putting its rulers on money. In 1866, Congress passed an amendment barring the “portrait or likeness” of living people from appearing on currency. That doesn’t appear to have bothered Trump. His scowling face dominates the new $1 coin, which is legal tender, and looks gold but is actually made from zinc, manganese, nickel and copper. It costs $61 to buy 25 one-dollar coins – you do the math – and about 9m of the coins are being made. They will, according to the US Mint, “honor 250 years of great American heritage”. That all sounds great, if you’re into that sort of thing, but what about the law?. Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, has argued that during the 150th celebration of America’s “birthday”, the face of then president Calvin Coolidge appeared on a coin, so during the 250th, the Trump coin is fine. The main problem seems to be that there’s a hodge-podge of laws which govern what can and cannot go on a coin. The 1866 ban on featuring living people arose from an impressively creative act of vanity. An incoming five-cent note was supposed to feature an image of the deceased explorer William Clark, but a treasury official called Spencer M Clark took advantage of the pair sharing a last name to instead print his own face on the note. The problem was that members of Congress a) noticed and b) were unamused. They passed an amendment which ruled that US money can only feature dead individuals – but it only applied to paper money. “For me, I would consider it illegal,” Gabriel Mathy, an associate professor of economics at American University who has studied American currency, said of the Trump coin. “But the United States has all these laws, which really are norms because they’re not really enforceable.” A deep dive into the policies, controversies and oddities surrounding the Trump administration The coin hasn’t been produced without a fight. In May, a group of Democratic members of Congress wrote to the treasury department in May, urging them to desist with the coin, pointing to a 2005 law which further restricted which presidents could appear on coins. And in March, James Rickher, a retired attorney in Portland, filed a request to block the coin, arguing it was illegal, but in June a federal judge denied that motion, writing that Rickher had “failed to present evidence that clearly shows he will personally suffer concrete harm from issuance of the challenged coin”, Fox 12 reported . The judge noted, however, that his ruling did not determine whether the coin is illegal or legal. And so today, Americans will be able to honor 250 years of great American heritage by buying a questionably legal one-dollar coin for roughly $2.44. If you’d like to know who came up with such a brilliant plan, just look at the coin.

events.title: Uber to cut 3,300 corporate jobs in management overhaul
events.summary: Company says it is slashing 10% of its workforce to make operations ‘simpler and faster’ Uber drivers launch European class action over ‘soulless’ and ‘scary’ AI algorithm Uber plans to cut its global workforce by about 10% as part of a major restructuring, slashing about 3,300 corporate jobs. The boss of the US-based ride-hailing app, Dara Khosrowshahi, told staff Wednesday that the changes would create a “simpler and faster” business by cutting layers of management and merging teams. Uber also plans to ask more employees to work in the office. Uber, which has its headquarters in San Francisco, did not specify how many roles would be affected in each location that it has offices, including in London. The cuts are the largest since 2020 when Uber laid off 6,700 people in response to a major downturn in rides during the Covid pandemic. Staff affected have been notified, but some countries will have their own local process to follow, according to the firm. Khosrowshahi said in his message that Uber had been growing in the past five years and the business was performing well. “But that growth has also brought complexity: more layers, more coordination, more fragmented ownership, and in some cases structures that made sense when businesses were smaller but no longer serve us well at our current scale,” he said. “The changes we’re making today are designed to do two things: make Uber simpler and faster, and create more capacity to invest in our future.” Uber is also asking the majority of its staff to come into an office, meaning less than about 1% of employees will be working remotely. The move will reinforce a hybrid work policy which requires three days a week in the office. Khosrowshahi laid out organisational changes including combining operational and tech teams, and reducing the number of “micro-teams” – where one or two employees report to a single manager – by nearly 50%. The number of employees who sit more than seven layers from the chief executive has also been cut by 20%. “The decisions we’re making today are difficult, but they will help us build an even stronger Uber for the years ahead,” Khosrowshahi said. Uber is preparing to launch self-driving taxis for the first time on UK roads after partnering with the robotaxi business Wayve and being granted approval by Transport for London last month. The company plans to spend $10bn toward developing its autonomous vehicle business, aiming to form a grip on the burgeoning market of self-driving. Uber also recently struck a $14.8bn deal to acquire the German company Delivery Hero as it jockeys for dominance in the global food delivery market. The company’s UberEats service faces intense competition from rival apps such as DoorDash. Uber expanded rapidly after launched in San Francisco in 2010 , and is now valued at more than $150bn.

events.title: How Kier Group’s Louisa Finlay is using Copilot to drive safety and productivity in the construction industry
events.summary: Copilot in the C-Suite -Sally Beatty Two years ago, Kier Group plc decided to embrace AI – with a little help from work friends and peers. Executives at the UK construction and infrastructure firm were excited by AI’s promise to boost productivity and enhance safety practices. But “some leaders were reticent because they were very busy and it is new technology,” says Louisa Finlay, chief operating officer of Kier . “I will happily be the one that asks the silly question,” she notes. “But if you are a senior leader, that can be quite worrying.” To encourage experimentation, executives and colleagues were invited to a series of “prompt-a-thons,” where they were encouraged to test their knowledge against AI. One team was asked to answer questions on their own, while a second team was asked to answer the same questions using Microsoft’s Copilot AI assistant . Separately, Kier encouraged AI adoption via fun prompts posed to multiple influencers and leaders throughout the company. Participants asked Copilot to review their emails, meeting documents and collaborations over the past six months and then identify which character they’d be in one of their favorite films. Colleagues who chose to participate enabled Copilot to identify participants’ leadership strengths and blind spots – and receive advice that would help them become more effective over the next 12 months. “The engagement following that was amazing,” says Finlay. By conducting the training in small peer groups, the prompt-a-thon “allowed people to feel comfortable not being the cleverest person in the room, knowing it’s OK to ask questions and not know the answers.” Since then, she says, Copilot use has “taken off.” Kier has roughly 11,000 employees and is based in Salford, England, not far from the northern industrial hub of Manchester. The company builds everything from schools to prisons and has a fast-growing infrastructure services division that builds and manages large-scale water and nuclear energy projects. About 40 percent of colleagues use Microsoft 365 Copilot ; the rest have Teams Premium , which adds advanced AI features to the Teams chat and meeting functions. Finlay uses Copilot within Outlook, Excel, Teams and PowerPoint. On any given day, she may ask Copilot to prioritize emails, conduct research or start the first draft of a job description. She also counts on Copilot for “joining the dots and giving you insights you wouldn’t get otherwise. It adds value to nearly everything I do day to day.” When not at work, she uses it to help plan travel itineraries and make up quizzes to entertain family and friends. Kier is also in the “early stages” of developing a series of AI agents. One is being developed to help collect and organize safety data that can be analyzed to help humans overseeing the agent to address possible risk areas and other forward-looking actions. Another is being trained on Kier safety standards and links to photographs documenting job sites, equipment and supplies, as well as drone video Kier collects from its vast construction portfolio. Drones, says Finlay, reduce the need for people to work at height or interact with “AI is supporting our people in their day-to-day activities, but we stress that they must be in control. We call it “Human at the Helm,” says Finlay. IT is developing an AI agent that is designed to speed up response times while still allowing people to quickly speak directly to a human as needed. . Data is securely stored on Microsoft’s Azure cloud platform. “We’re trying to make it easy for people to be productive and safe,” says Finlay. Kier is also looking to deploy AI in its facilities management business, to help predict when complex building parts, such as pumps or elevators, might need servicing to help support continuity of operation. Training colleagues to use AI with confidence While Finlay believes AI and robotics have huge potential to boost efficiency and productivity across the construction business, and make job sites safer, “we still need to bring on new graduates and apprentices” to learn the trade from the ground up and supervise more routine work that is increasingly being handled by AI. Training colleagues throughout the company to be comfortable using AI is a top priority for Finlay. She believes people learn more and enjoy small group peer learning sessions, such as prompt-a-thons, over webinars or other computer-based training sessions that individuals do on their own. Next steps include sharing more colleague stories inside the company, so people can learn from each other in a “safe environment,” and responding to ideas submitted by employees about new ways to apply AI at work. Finlay was particularly gratified to receive an email from a site manager who happens to be dyslexic thanking her for rolling out AI and telling her using Copilot was “game changing” for him. “With Copilot and AI, we want people to know this is about people solving their own problems. It’s not being done to them,” says Finlay. “The biggest skill we can ask from everybody these days is curiosity and being willing to try new things,” she adds. “You know, ‘What is it? Can I try it?” Sally Beatty writes about AI and innovation at Microsoft, focusing on the company’s most cutting-edge breakthroughs and how emerging technologies are improving the lives of ordinary people. Previously, Sally was a feature reporter for the Wall Street Journal in New York, where she broke news about media and marketing. A California native, Sally lived in Hong Kong in the early 1990s, where she wrote for the Journal about the societal impact of economic and political reforms and consumer spending trends. events.title: Warren Buffett piled into Alphabet to bet big on AI, successor Greg Abel says
events.summary: Warren Buffett is Berkshire Hathaway's chairman and former CEO. Bloomberg/Getty Images Warren Buffett bet big on Alphabet to gain exposure to the AI boom, Greg Abel says. Berkshire Hathaway's new CEO said Buffett is still weighing in on big decisions at the company. Abel said he consulted with Buffett before taking part in Alphabet's stock offering this year. Warren Buffett bet on Alphabet to tap into the AI boom, and he's still helping to call the shots at Berkshire Hathaway, Greg Abel says. The legendary investor was succeeded by Abel at the start of this year after nearly six decades as Berkshire's CEO. During a rare on-air interview with CNBC on Wednesday, Abel shed light on Buffett's surprising tech bet and his ongoing role as chairman . The Berkshire CEO explained why Buffett built a nearly $38 billion stake in Alphabet from scratch in under a year. Google's parent company was the third-largest position in Berkshire's stock portfolio at the end of June . Abel pointed to AI's material impact on businesses and beyond, Berkshire having a " lot of visibility " into AI and its benefits through its myriad subsidiaries, and Alphabet being a "significant player" in the space. "Now there's a lot more to Google than what I just said in why we like it, but those were the fundamental reasons as to why we took a serious look at Google, and now have a significant investment in it," Abel said. Berkshire bolstered its Alphabet stake earlier this year by participating in a private placement. Abel said Berkshire was invited in late May to take part, and he promptly called Buffett to discuss the opportunity. Consulting with his predecessor was "very much consistent with how we manage Berkshire," Abel said. The pair agreed on a $10 billion investment at a 6.5% discount to Alphabet's market price, Abel said, and the transaction went ahead . Buffett has eschewed tech companies for most of his career, preferring to invest in more predictable, attractively valued businesses he understands deeply. But Alphabet and Berkshire have some shared DNA. Alphabet's bosses modeled it on Berkshire and its web of decentralized, autonomous subsidiaries after visiting Buffett in Omaha in the mid-2000s. In addition to Google, Alphabet is the parent company of YouTube, Android, Waymo, and others. Google's cofounders, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, also said that Buffett's essays and "owner's manual" for Berkshire shareholders were the main inspirations for the shareholder letter they included in Google's 2004 IPO prospectus. Buffett previously broke from tradition when he bought into Apple in 2016. The iPhone maker has proven to be one of his most successful investments , and remains Berkshire's biggest stock position. Buffett and Abel The Alphabet position is one of many topics of discussion for Berkshire's chairman and its CEO, Abel said. He and Buffett have a " great working relationship ," he told CNBC, and speak regularly as "we love talking business, we love talking about what we're seeing across our portfolio." Berkshire owns scores of businesses, including See's Candies and Geico, and holds multibillion-dollar stakes in public companies such as American Express and Coca-Cola. Abel, speaking from Japan during a visit to Berkshire's business interests there, told CNBC that he stopped by Buffett's 96th birthday celebration in Omaha on Sunday, and sensed some FOMO from the business icon. "Warren absolutely loves the Japanese investments," Abel said, "so I could tell it wasn't easy for Warren that off I went to Tokyo." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A cook who grew up on the Mediterranean Diet shares what she eats in a day, including sweet potatoes at breakfast
events.summary: Suzy Karadsheh is from Port Said, Egypt. The Mediterranean Dish Suzy Karadsheh grew up following the Mediterranean Diet in Port Said, Egypt. The city's cuisine is influenced by nearby countries, including Greece, Turkey, and Italy. Karadsheh eats a savory breakfast and cooks dinner in 45 minutes or less. Growing up in the Egyptian city of Port Said, Suzy Karadsheh and her dad would head to the local market after school every day to pick up fresh produce for dinner. Once at home, she would do her homework in the kitchen, inhaling the fragrant garlicky, spicy, or tomatoey aromas as her mom cooked dinner. The port city borders the Mediterranean Sea , making its local cuisine a melting pot of flavors from Egypt as well as nearby countries, including Greece, Turkey, and Italy. "I was taking it in without realizing," Karadsheh, the founder of The Mediterranean Dish, a recipe website, told Business Insider. Now based in Atlanta and a busy mom of two, Karadsheh no longer has time to visit the local market every day, but she applies the principles of the Mediterranean diet to the 45-minute meals she makes for her and her family each day. The Mediterranean diet is widely considered the healthiest way to eat . It prioritizes seasonal fruit and vegetables, legumes, whole grains, fish, and extra-virgin olive oil, but isn't rigid. "It's a joyful way to eat. It is not a restrictive way to eat. And I think people miss that when they hear the word diet in Mediterranean diet," she said. She does have one rule, though: "not spending more than a half-hour prepping on a weeknight," she said. Karadsheh shared what she eats on a typical day following the Mediterranean diet. Savory breakfast Karadsheh eats a late breakfast. nubphan koi/Getty Images "I grew up with a savory breakfast . So we don't do sugary breakfast in this house very much," Karadsheh said. For breakfast, she often eats sweet potatoes, which she roasts in advance and stores in the fridge, with fried eggs. To make the breakfast, she cuts a pre-cooked sweet potato in half, grills both halves on a skillet with a bit of olive oil, and sears them for about three minutes until they are warmed throughout. In the same skillet, she fries two eggs. She plates them up and usually pairs them with some chopped cucumber and tomatoes, and feta cheese. "It is just so filling," she said. Mediterranean grain bowl for lunch Lunch is a low-key affair for Karadsheh because she often has a late breakfast. She typically has leftovers or uses the precooked grains and roasted veggies she keeps in her fridge to make a Mediterranean grain bowl. She often has some hummus and a piece of bread on the side. Whole grains are central to the Mediterranean diet, and a great source of fiber . One cup of cooked quinoa, for example, contains five grams of fiber. Karadsheh's favorite grains are freekeh, a roasted durum wheat with a "savory and smoky flavor" popular in Egypt, and farro, an ancient Italian grain. Winner winner chicken (or fish) dinner Karadsheh makes marinades inspired by different Mediterranean countries. DronG/Getty Images This summer, Karadsheh has mostly been eating fish or chicken with a Greek salad, containing bell peppers, tomato, cucumber, good feta cheese, onions, and olives, plus some grains, and sometimes tzatziki, a yogurt sauce. Her go-to fish recipe is an oven-baked lemon, garlic cod. To make it, she dips the cod in a lemon, olive oil , and butter sauce, then coats it in flour seasoned with paprika, cumin, coriander, and salt. Next, she sears the fish in an iron cast skillet to give it some color, pours over the rest of the lemon sauce with some minced garlic, and cooks it in the oven for 10 to 15 minutes at 400 °F. She loves trying out marinades for grilled chicken too, taking inspiration from different Mediterranean countries. Sometimes it's harissa, a Tunisian hot chili paste, she said, other times it might be Greek oregano, lemon juice, and olive oil. Gut health experts recommend aiming to eat 30 different types of plant foods a week, as research suggests this number promotes healthy diversity in the gut microbiome, the trillions of microbes that live in the colon lining and impact overall health. Using plenty of herbs and spices, which all count as different plants, is an easy way to get closer to the coveted 30 plants a week. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Wonderful more than doubles its valuation to $5B in under 6 months
events.summary: Israeli-Dutch AI startup Wonderful has raised $550 million in a Series C funding round that gives it a price tag of $5 billion, more than doubling the $2 billion valuation the company gained when it last raised funding nearly six months ago . Insight Partners returned to lead this round, too, and existing investors Index Ventures, IVP, Vine Ventures, 9Yards, and Bessemer Venture Partners are participating once again. Salesforce is investing in the company for the first time in this round. Founded in early 2025, Wonderful has grown blazingly fast. It initially saw strong traction with its customer service AI agent platform, which it built and customized to sell in various non-English-speaking markets. Its strategy of deploying engineering teams to work with its customers, sometimes on their premises, to deploy and integrate its AI tech into their workflows and systems also proved very successful. The company says it now works across more than 35 countries. The startup’s core offering has evolved over the past few months, though. Departing from its customer service roots, Wonderful now offers a platform, dubbed “Wonderful AI OS,” which it says can coordinate and connect agents, workflows, and AI applications with companies’ data, context, and existing integrations. The company says the platform works with any AI model and is compatible with existing tech stacks. “Customers can adopt whichever parts of the platform make the most sense, integrate them with existing systems, choose the best models for each workload, and retain ownership of everything they build,” Roey Lalazar, Wonderful CTO and co-founder, said in a statement. The company is still leaning on its forward-deployed engineers to help embed its products quickly into companies — which appears to be a good strategy given the demand for experts versed in implementing AI services and products. Wonderful said it will use the fresh $550 million to develop products faster, expand its FDE teams, and meet demand for its products. events.title: India’s richest man now wants to turn aging computers into AI-ready PCs
events.summary: Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Jio is opening its cloud PC service to any internet user in India, positioning it as a way to turn aging computers into AI-ready machines without hardware upgrades. On Wednesday, Reliance Jio expanded JioPC, originally launched in July 2025, beyond its own broadband subscribers, making the service available as a stand-alone subscription to users with an internet connection, regardless of their telecom or broadband provider. The service streams a virtual PC from Jio’s cloud to an existing computer, with plans offering up to eight virtual CPUs, 16GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage. Jio says the service can give even computers as old as eight years access to the computing power needed for modern AI applications, without users replacing their machines or installing new hardware. Plans start at ₹1,000 (about $11) for two months, while a 12-month subscription costs ₹4,000 (around $42) for 8GB of RAM and 500GB of storage, or ₹5,000 (about $53) for the 16GB and 1TB configuration. India had more than 65 million PCs in use in 2025, including about 34 million consumer and 31 million commercial machines, according to estimates from IDC, which expects the installed base to approach 69 million by the end of 2026. Ambani’s move comes amid widening replacement cycles. Consumers and small businesses in India typically replace their PCs every five to six years, compared with four to five years in 2022, IDC’s senior market analyst Bharath Shenoy told TechCrunch. Enterprises are stretching their machines for longer too, with replacement cycles reaching about four years, up from three previously. Jio is betting that cloud computing can stretch those lifecycles further. By shifting much of the processing and storage away from the device and into its data centers, India’s most valuable company can keep adding computing capacity without requiring users to replace the machines sitting on their desks. Prabhu Ram, vice president of the industry research group at the Gurugram-based market analyst firm CyberMedia Research, said JioPC could instead create a market where consumers pay for computing capability rather than repeatedly spending on hardware upgrades. “Jio is broadening its value proposition by opening JioPC to non-Jio users, while also challenging the traditional hardware upgrade cycle,” Ram told TechCrunch. However, he does not expect that model to replace conventional PCs. JioPC, he noted, could create a parallel, price-sensitive tier for households, students, and others “for whom buying a new AI-capable PC was never really on the table to begin with.” Indians have traditionally preferred owning their hardware over paying for PCs as a service, Shenoy said. Jio will have to convince consumers that a recurring subscription is worth giving up some of the advantages of a conventional PC, including the ability to keep working without the internet. That dependence could be particularly prominent in the smaller cities and towns where affordable computing has the most room to grow. JioPC requires a stable internet connection, and any disruption can affect the user experience, unlike a conventional computer. Additionally, there is competition at the low end from refurbished PCs, which Shenoy said allow consumers to own inexpensive hardware without remaining dependent on connectivity. Jio’s pitch of an “AI-ready” PC through JioPC also challenges the conventional idea of what an AI PC looks like. The company has not disclosed much about the underlying hardware powering the cloud service. However, the specifications it has provided do not mention dedicated AI accelerators for on-device generative AI workloads, which is a key feature of the new generation of AI PCs. Moreover, the real test for Jio, Ram said, is whether people come to see cloud computing as a “daily utility” rather than an “opportunistic workaround,” and are willing to pay for computing power instead of buying new hardware. events.title: El Niño threatens West Africa's cocoa producers
events.summary: West Africa’s cocoa producers are under threat from this year’s El Niño, which threatens to be the worst on record. The weather phenomenon has been known to intensify the yearly Harmattan winds, which dry out topsoil and cause pods to fall. Côte d’Ivoire — the world’s top producer — is expected to see its output slump by around a fifth , Bloomberg reported. El Niño is likely to exacerbate the impact of torrential rains in neighboring Ghana that have damaged crops and increased the prevalence of the plant-killing black pod disease. The Institute of International Finance warned that cocoa is not the only food product at risk from El Niño, which forecasts suggest will affect Africa’s agricultural sector across the board, through either flooding or drought. Projections suggest the extreme weather patterns will drive food inflation across much of the continent. Many African economies are in a much weaker economic position compared to the strong 2015-2016 El Niño, the IIF report said, largely due to higher oil prices, which have driven up transport costs, and a strong US dollar. — Paige Bruton

events.title: The Logical End Point of AI Job Interviews Is Two Bots Talking to Each Other
events.summary: Christopher has become accustomed to jumping through the endless hoops of the modern job hunt. Like many government contractors, his work has dried up in the DOGE era . Over the past six months, he has applied to roughly 700 jobs; in the vast majority of cases, he’s heard nothing back. Five of these applications have gone through “Riley,” an AI recruiter for the IT firm Everforth Apex Systems. The first time Riley reached out, Christopher was excited. It was June, and he had by then realized how difficult the job market was. (Christopher asked that WIRED use only his first name as his job hunt continues.) A text from Riley felt like a rare opportunity to pitch himself, even if his interlocutor was virtual. During his first call with Riley, Christopher answered questions about his work authorization and his professional background. Riley promised that, if Christopher met the qualifications, someone would be in touch. But a human recruiter never reached out. Nor did the AI agent—until a little over a week later, when Riley texted Christopher about “another opportunity.” Christopher hoped he could improve upon his original interview. So he set up another call with the AI agent. Then again for another job. And another. None of the interviews resulted in any follow-up conversations or emails; he never even received an automated rejection text. By the fifth time Riley texted him, Christopher had had enough. If the company was going to use AI, he reasoned, why shouldn’t he do the same? Christopher typed a handful of sentences of background information into ChatGPT Voice and told it to stand in as “Christopher.” Then, Christopher says, when Riley called, “I just put them next to each other, and they just hit it off.” The call lasted 10 minutes. Riley told ChatGPT it was “great talking to you.” ChatGPT said it appreciated “how clear and straightforward the process was.” During one particularly entertaining sequence, the bots tried to nail down a potential start date and got trapped in a circular conversation about “standard onboarding and background checks.” Riley promised that a recruiter would reach out if the application met the company’s qualifications, just as she had the other four times. Again, a recruiter never materialized. It was, as Christopher calls it, a “slop flywheel.” “This is one synthetic persona giving slop data to another synthetic persona,” he says. “And all of the data is going—where? Nowhere.” The exercise was a mix of “mischievous fun” and frustration, Christopher says, as well as “a dismissal of ever wanting to work” with this company. Everforth Apex Systems did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. Though AI has seeped into every step of the job hunt for both applicants and recruiters, it has taken time to catch on in interviews. Voice AI is infamously tricky to pull off, as agents get tripped up by accents or “ums.” Behavior that would be second nature to a human—like not interrupting a candidate—turns into a “very, very difficult engineering problem,” according to Ophir Samson, the head of voice AI at recruitment platform Greenhouse. But recruiters, overwhelmed with the glut of applications, have increasingly turned to voice AI tools to screen candidates, with 63 percent of job seekers reporting they’ve encountered an AI interview, according to Greenhouse. As recruiters turned to AI, so did applicants. Candidates using AI in the interview process has become so common that AI recruitment startups like Ribbon promise to help identify “overly scripted, AI-assisted, or coached” responses—just like those in Christopher’s experiment. Now there are rumblings that bot-on-bot interviews aren’t duplicitous but a preview of things to come. In many ways, it’s the “next logical stage,” Mark Monaghan, vice president of organizational development at call center company IQor, tells WIRED. That doesn’t mean he’s entirely happy about it. In Christopher’s case, Monaghan believes, the use of AI was more than justified. “If you’re going to send a bot to me,” he says, “I’ll send a bot to you.” After his fifth interview with no follow-up, Christopher decided to apply for one more Everforth Apex job. Perhaps, Christopher thought, the problem wasn’t AI. Maybe it was him. Maybe if Riley were able to speak to the company’s dream candidate, things would go differently. So he created a fake candidate, whom he called Don Dickner, packing a résumé to the brim with qualifications pulled from an open job posting. After Christopher submitted the application, Riley immediately reached out. This time, the virtual recruiter spoke with ChatGPT—posing as Dickner—for 23 minutes. They discussed “sustainable operational improvement,” protecting “customer experience under volume pressure,” and refusing to let “tribal knowledge drift.” ChatGPT had an answer for every question, and a personal anecdote for every qualification. As the interview wrapped up, ChatGPT said it had a “few more questions I’d like answered.

events.title: Nigerian opposition vows to restore fuel subsidy
events.summary: The scrapping of Nigeria’s fuel subsidy by President Bola Tinubu’s administration has emerged as a key battleground ahead of the country’s elections. The opposition African Democratic Congress said it will anchor its campaign on a promise to reinstate the multibillion-dollar program, whose removal three years ago drove up food and transportation prices to create a cost-of-living crisis that still persists in Africa’s most populous country. ADC is the party of Atiku Abubakar, a former Nigerian vice president who is one of two leading challengers to Tinubu in the presidential poll to be held in four months. He has pledged to restore a “ targeted subsidy ” that would differ from the one Tinubu removed, a move his party said is justified “because Nigerians are too poor not to be subsidised.” Abuja argues that the removal of the fuel subsidy, which cost $10 billion in 2022 — the year before Tinubu took office — was needed to reduce the country’s yawning budget deficit and that shelving it has led to a higher amount of revenue distributed monthly to states. The IMF last year credited the subsidy removal as one reason for Nigeria’s “ improved macroeconomic stability and enhanced resilience.” — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: Lutnick: Anthropic is "back on the right side" with Trump administration
events.summary: CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the Trump administration now trusts Anthropic following months of clashes with the AI company. Why it matters: The statement marks a remarkable turnaround in a relationship strained by a bitter fight over national security and AI safeguards . What they're saying: Asked if he trusts Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Lutnick told Axios' Mike Allen: "We trust Anthropic." "They've done what we asked. They're back on the right side. So the answer is: Yes," Lutnick said in an interview on Tuesday. The big picture: The declaration comes as Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown takes a more prominent role in the company's relationship with the White House, including a headlining spot at this week's G20 Innovation Ministerial . "Really excited for our conversation, so I'd like to introduce you all to Tom Brown, one of the founders of Anthropic," Lutnick said on Wednesday to a room full of G20 ministers. Lutnick kicked off the discussion offering Brown an opportunity to introduce himself to an international audience: "I don't think they know you so well. Anthropic, of course, is famous, but a little story helps." What they're saying: Brown praised President Trump's pro-data center post on Truth Social this week. "I really love Trump's post from earlier this week... where he was pointing out that the data centers are just an enormous source of prosperity," Brown said. "They produce a ton of jobs. They produce taxes. Now the way that we design them, we actually bring on more power to the grid," he said. Brown also highlighted Anthropic's support for the administration's ratepayer pledge. Between the lines: Industry knows aligning with the Trump administration goes a long way for policy priorities. Catch up quick: Personality differences added fuel to the fire in a clash between the Trump administration and Anthropic earlier this year that resulted in sweeping export controls on the company's most advanced models. Brown was instrumental in patching up the relationship, holding multiple conversations with Lutnick and National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. A federal judge in August, meanwhile, struck down the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk , ruling that the government's actions violated Anthropic's constitutional rights. The company is also fighting a separate Pentagon designation under a different statute in the D.C. Circuit. The bottom line: Brown offers a reset for a company once on the outs with the White House.
